Mitre
MY-ter
n.
Greek mitra, “headband, turban”; Hebrew mits’nepheth, “turban,” from tsānaph, “to wrap, wind around.” The headdress of the Old Testament high priest, a fine linen wrapping over the head, on the front of which was fastened the gold plate engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD.

📖 Biblical Definition

The mitre was the headdress of the Old Testament high priest—a fine linen wrapping or turban worn over the head, on the front of which was fastened a gold plate engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD (Hebrew qōdesh la-YHWH). Exodus 28:36-38 prescribes the mitre and its plate: and thou shalt make a plate of pure gold, and grave upon it, like the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD. And thou shalt put it on a blue lace, that it may be upon the mitre; upon the forefront of the mitre it shall be. And it shall be upon Aaron’s forehead, that Aaron may bear the iniquity of the holy things, which the children of Israel shall hallow in all their holy gifts; and it shall be always upon his forehead, that they may be accepted before the LORD. Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, the inscription: HOLINESS TO THE LORD—the gold plate proclaimed the very purpose of the priestly office and of Israel’s separation as a holy nation. Second, the location: the forefront of the mitre, on Aaron’s forehead, the most visible place on the high priest’s body, so that the inscription faced every Israelite who looked upon the priest. Third, the function: the plate is explicitly tied to bearing the iniquity of the holy things, that the offerings may be accepted before the LORD. The high priest, wearing the plate of holiness on his forehead, sanctified the offerings of the people; their gifts, presented through him under the inscription of holiness to the LORD, were accepted on account of the priestly bearing of any iniquity that adhered to the offerings. Fourth, the typological substance. Christ is the great High Priest who fulfills the mitre-and-plate symbolism: He bears the iniquity of the holy things, sanctifying the offerings of His people, presenting them acceptable to the Father through His own perfect holiness. Hebrews 7:26 names His qualification: for such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens. The plate of pure gold engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD finds its substantive fulfillment in the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, whose person is the very Holiness to the LORD that the inscription proclaimed. And there is an eschatological echo: in the New Jerusalem, the saints themselves shall bear the name: and there shall be no more curse: but the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it; and his servants shall serve him: And they shall see his face; and his name shall be in their foreheads (Rev 22:3-4); cf. Rev 14:1 of the 144,000 having his Father’s name written in their foreheads. The mitre-plate, originally on the high priest’s forehead, finds its consummate fulfillment in the name of God written on the foreheads of all His redeemed in the New Jerusalem.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines MITRE as a sacerdotal ornament worn on the head by bishops and certain abbots on solemn occasions; in scripture (rendering mits’nepheth), the linen headdress of the Old Testament high priest, on the front of which was fastened the gold plate engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD.

MITRE, n. — 1. A sacerdotal ornament worn on the head by bishops and certain abbots on solemn occasions. 2. In scripture, the headdress of the Jewish high priest, a fine linen turban with the gold plate engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD fastened to its front (Ex 28:36-38).

HOLINESS, n. — The state of being holy; purity or integrity of moral character; separation from sin and consecration to God.

📖 Key Scripture

Exodus 28:36-38 — "And thou shalt make a plate of pure gold, and grave upon it, like the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD. And thou shalt put it on a blue lace, that it may be upon the mitre; upon the forefront of the mitre it shall be. And it shall be upon Aaron’s forehead, that Aaron may bear the iniquity of the holy things, which the children of Israel shall hallow in all their holy gifts; and it shall be always upon his forehead, that they may be accepted before the LORD."

Leviticus 8:9 — "And he put the mitre upon his head; also upon the mitre, even upon his forefront, did he put the golden plate, the holy crown; as the LORD commanded Moses."

Hebrews 7:26 — "For such an high priest became us, who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners, and made higher than the heavens."

Revelation 22:3-4 — "And there shall be no more curse: but the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it; and his servants shall serve him: And they shall see his face; and his name shall be in their foreheads."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The mitre-doctrine is corrupted by the broader contemporary loss of priestly typology that has reduced the high priest’s vestments to ancient cultic curiosity without tracing their Christological substance—and by the inverse over-extension in some sacerdotal traditions that have used the mitre’s historical existence to justify elaborate post-apostolic priestly vestments and offices the New Testament does not warrant.

expand to see more

The general loss of priestly typology affects the mitre as it does the broader Aaronic vestments. The high priest’s mitre, ephod, breastplate, robe, coat, and girdle are richly symbolic of the priestly office and of the great High Priest who fulfills them all in Christ. Where the typology is lost, these are treated as ancient ceremonial detail without the substantive Christological connection. The recovery is the recovery of the controlling NT typology in Hebrews 4-10: Christ is the High Priest who is holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners; His person is the very Holiness to the LORD that the mitre-plate proclaimed; He bears the iniquity of the holy things, sanctifying the offerings of His people, presenting them acceptable to the Father. The mitre-plate doctrine is therefore not ancient cultic detail but a structural Christological-and-pastoral substance: Christ’s holiness, borne in the most visible place, sanctifying every offering the saint brings through Him.

The opposite corruption is the over-extension in some sacerdotal traditions (Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, certain high-Anglican) that have used the mitre’s biblical existence to justify elaborate post-apostolic priestly vestments and offices the New Testament does not warrant. Bishops wearing mitres in the present church carry forward an Old Testament priestly category that the New Testament has not transferred to post-apostolic church officers. The NT recognizes elders/overseers and deacons (1 Tim 3; Tit 1) without any reinstitution of the Aaronic priesthood or its distinctive vestments. The priesthood under the New Covenant is the priesthood of all believers (1 Pet 2:9, but ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood) under the one High Priest Jesus Christ; the elaborate vestments and the bishop’s mitre of medieval-and-later church order are post-apostolic developments not warranted in the NT text. Recover both ends. Refuse the loss of typology that drops the mitre-doctrine altogether, and refuse the over-extension that perpetuates Aaronic vestments in post-apostolic offices. The biblical doctrine is Christological: Christ is the Holy One whose holiness, like the mitre-plate, sanctifies the offerings of His people, and the saints under the new covenant are the priesthood whose holiness derives from their union with Him.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mits’nepheth (turban, mitre), from tsānaph (to wrap); Greek mitra (headband, turban); the high priest’s linen headdress with the gold plate engraved HOLINESS TO THE LORD; typologically fulfilled in Christ’s person as the great High Priest whose holiness sanctifies the offerings of His people.

expand to see more

Hebrew mits’nepheth (H4701) — turban, mitre (the high priest’s headdress).

Hebrew tsānaph (H6801) — to wrap, wind around (the verb behind the noun).

Hebrew tsits (H6731) — blossom, plate (the gold plate fastened to the front of the mitre, also called the nēzer, holy crown).

Greek archiereus (G749) — high priest (the NT title applied to Christ in Hebrews).

Usage

"HOLINESS TO THE LORD—the engraved gold plate on the mitre’s forefront proclaimed the very purpose of the priestly office."

"The mitre-plate sanctified the offerings of the people, the high priest bearing the iniquity of the holy things so that the gifts might be accepted before the LORD."

"Christ’s holy person fulfills the mitre-plate: His holiness sanctifies every offering His people bring through Him; the consummation is the name of God on every redeemed saint’s forehead in the New Jerusalem."
